theta-true-false.title: Θ-Notation: Decide Whether the Classes Match
theta-true-false.bodyMarkdown:
Treat `Θ(h(n))` as the set of functions that grow at the same asymptotic rate as `h(n)`.

- `Θ(n²) = Θ(n² + 7)` — **True.** The constant `7` is lower order.
- `Θ(n²) = Θ(7n²)` — **True.** A positive constant factor does not change the class.
- `Θ(7n² + 18) = Θ(n²)` — **True.** The quadratic term dominates the constant.
- `Θ(n² + n) = Θ(n²)` — **True.** The linear term is lower order.
- `Θ(n²) = Θ(n³)` — **False.** Their ratio `n²/n³ = 1/n` tends to zero.

### Quick test

Factor or divide by the proposed representative. If the ratio tends to a positive finite constant, the classes match. If it tends to zero or infinity, they do not.

theta-equivalence-animation.title: Strip Constants and Lower-Order Terms
theta-equivalence-animation.context: The animation shows what Θ notation ignores—and what it does not.

steps.title: Remove positive constant factors
steps.body: 7n² and n² differ by a fixed multiplier, so they share a Θ class.

steps.title: Ignore lower-order additions
steps.body: n²+7 and n²+n both have n² as the dominant term.

steps.title: Do not merge different powers
steps.body: n²/n³=1/n tends to zero, so the classes are different.
